name: ReversalWithoutTouchingResistanceIsStrongSign
quote: Whenever a market turns back down without touching a resistance level, the bears are very strong because they are not waiting for the resistance to be touched.
description: Filter: a reversal that begins before price even reaches a nearby remembered resistance level is a stronger with-trend signal than one that waits for the level to be tested.
pseudocode: highest(high, sinceSignalLookback) < resistanceLevel - untouchedTicks * tickSize && close[0] < open[0]

complexity.reason: needs a remembered resistance level and confirmation that price never reached it

chapter_title: Signs of Strength in a Breakout

name: MagnetProximityIncreasesReversalOdds
quote: The closer the market gets to any magnet, the stronger the magnetic field and the more likely the market will reach the magnet (this is the basis for buy and sell vacuums).
description: Context filter: weight reversal/target-completion entries more heavily as price gets within nearTicks of a known magnet level (an unfilled gap midpoint, breakout point, or similar remembered level).
book_order_type: n/a (confidence weighting, not an order by itself)

complexity.reason: 'magnet' and 'vacuum' are qualitative; a design decision is needed on which remembered levels count and how proximity should weight other signals

notes: Chapter 10 (Other Magnets) is the fuller treatment; this chapter's contribution is only the proximity-increases-odds framing.

name: FibonacciRetracementLevel
description: Shared primitive: a Fibonacci retracement/projection ratio (e.g., 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%) of the most recent swing acts as a support/resistance magnet.
pseudocode: swingHigh = mostRecentSwingHigh(pivotStrength); swingLow = mostRecentSwingLow(pivotStrength); level = swingHigh - fibRatio * (swingHigh - swingLow); abs(close[0] - level) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to anchor the retracement, and which ratio to use is itself a choice

notes: Book merely lists this as a common S/R type; gives no worked example in this chapter.
chapter_title: Part II: Magnets: Support and Resistance

name: TradeTowardUnreachedMagnetOnlyFilter
quote: When you become aware of a magnet not too far from the current price, trade only in the direction of the magnet until after it is reached.
description: Filter: while a known price magnet lies within magnetRangeTicks ahead in the current direction and has not yet been touched, permit only entries toward that magnet; block fresh countertrend entries until it is reached.
pseudocode: distanceToMagnet = abs(nearestUnreachedMagnetLevel - close[0]); distanceToMagnet <= magnetRangeTicks * tickSize && !magnetReachedYet => blockCountertrendEntry

complexity.reason: requires a design decision on which remembered levels qualify as 'the' magnet and how 'reached' is defined

notes: Book immediately qualifies this: 'there still can be reliable trades in both directions' before the magnet is reached, so this is a soft bias, not a hard block.
chapter_title: Part II: Magnets: Support and Resistance

name: WeakMoveTowardMagnetAgainstTrendFade
quote: If the move toward the magnet is weak and if it is against the direction of a larger trend, you can also look to initiate a trade in the opposite direction, expecting a reversal.
description: When price approaches a known magnet counter to the larger trend with weak (small-bodied, overlapping) bars, enter with the larger trend expecting a reversal at the magnet.
pseudocode: distanceToMagnet <= magnetRangeTicks * tickSize && avgBodyFraction(recentBars) <= weakBodyFraction && counterToLargerTrend

complexity.reason: needs a magnet level, a larger-trend-context read, and a 'weak move' bar-quality test together

chapter_title: Part II: Magnets: Support and Resistance

name: SecondReversalAtMagnetEntry
quote: If the trend resumes and goes even further past the magnet and then reverses a second time, this is usually a reliable setup for a trade in the opposite direction, especially if there is a strong reversal bar.
description: After price first overshoots a magnet and reverses, then resumes and overshoots the magnet a second time, a strong reversal bar on the second overshoot is a reliable countertrend entry.
book_order_type: stop entry beyond the second reversal bar

complexity.reason: needs a remembered magnet level and a persistent count of prior overshoot-and-reversal events at it

notes: A magnet-specific instance of the general 'second entries are more reliable' idea also seen in Chapter 5 (double top/bottom, H2/L2).
chapter_title: Part II: Magnets: Support and Resistance

name: SupportResistanceRoleFlipPrimitive
quote: Once the market falls through support, it usually becomes resistance; and once the market breaks above resistance, it usually becomes support.
description: Shared primitive: once a remembered support level is broken (closed below), relabel it as a resistance level for future tests from below (and mirror for resistance broken to the upside).
pseudocode: if wasSupport(level) && close[0] < level - toleranceTicks * tickSize: level.role = resistance
book_order_type: n/a (level-state transition, feeds other S/R-based rules)

complexity.reason: needs a persistent level object with a role flag that flips on a qualifying break

notes: Applies to any of the level primitives above (moving average, trend line, trading-range boundary, etc.).
chapter_title: Part II: Magnets: Support and Resistance

name: RecentSwingExtremeMagnet
quote: Swing highs and lows of the past few bars or even days, often setting up double bottom bull flags and double top bear flags.
description: A recent swing high or low (within the last N bars/days) is a magnet the market is often drawn back to test, frequently forming a double top or double bottom there.
pseudocode: swingLevel = highest(high, lookback)[1] (or lowest(low, lookback)[1] for the mirror); high[0] >= swingLevel - toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: a highest/lowest window is enough as a proxy for a recent swing extreme

notes: Overlaps with the double top / double bottom family formalized in Chapter 12; dedup pass should merge.

name: HigherTimeframeSwingAndMaMagnet
quote: Daily, weekly, and monthly swing highs and lows, bar highs and lows, moving averages, gaps, Fibonacci retracements and extensions, and trend lines.
description: Swing highs/lows, bar extremes, moving averages, gaps, and trend lines computed on a higher time frame (daily/weekly/monthly) of the same instrument act as magnets for the traded time frame.
pseudocode: higherTfLevel = swing/MA/gap/trend-line level computed on a resampled higher-timeframe series of the same instrument; abs(close[0] - higherTfLevel) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs a design decision on whether/how the engine exposes a resampled higher-timeframe data series

name: FibonacciRetracementMagnet
quote: Daily, weekly, and monthly swing highs and lows, bar highs and lows, moving averages, gaps, Fibonacci retracements and extensions, and trend lines.
description: Fibonacci retracement/extension levels (e.g. 50%, 61.8%, 127%, 161.8%) of the most recent swing act as magnets for pullbacks and projections.
pseudocode: swingHigh = highest(high, lookback)[1]; swingLow = lowest(low, lookback)[1]; fibLevel = swingHigh - fibRatio * (swingHigh - swingLow); abs(close[0] - fibLevel) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to anchor the ratio

notes: Kept separate from R10-16 because the ratio arithmetic, not just data availability, is the extra piece here.

name: RoundNumberMagnet
quote: Round numbers like hundreds in stocks (e.g., AAPL at $300) and thousands in the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow 12,000). If a stock quickly moves from $50 to $88, it will likely try to test $100 and usually go to $105 or $110 before pulling back.
description: Round-number price levels (multiples of roundStep) act as magnets; price is often drawn to the nearest one and may overshoot slightly beyond it before pulling back.
pseudocode: nearestRound = round(close[0] / roundStep) * roundStep; abs(close[0] - nearestRound) <= toleranceTicks * tickSize
book_order_type: n/a (level construction; take profits into it or expect a slight overshoot)

complexity.reason: modular price arithmetic, no window needed

notes: roundStep is instrument-specific (100 for a $300 stock, 1000 for the Dow).

name: MagnetFailureRetestSetup
quote: Failure to reach a magnet, like a measured move target, a prior swing high or low, a trend line, or a trend channel line. This often leads to a pullback and then another attempt to reach the magnet.
description: When price comes close to but fails to reach a magnet (measured-move target, prior swing extreme, or trend line) and pulls back, expect a renewed push back toward that magnet; trade the pullback in the direction of the original move.
pseudocode: // needs a design decision on how 'magnet' targets (measured moves, swing extremes, trend/channel lines) are represented before a concrete test can be written
book_order_type: n/a (setup concept, not a specific order)

complexity.reason: the concept is real but requires deciding how to represent measured-move / trend-line 'magnets' before any bar-level test can be coded

notes: Ties together several already-hard primitives (measured moves, trend lines) around a single failure/retest idea.

name: MagnetTestBeforeFade
quote: with its high so close to the moving average, they would have felt more confident about their shorts if the market first touched the moving average ... Many would not have looked to short until after the moving average was touched.
description: Filter: a fade entry at the EMA (or another magnet) is allowed only once price has actually touched that level, not merely approached within a tick of it.
book_order_type: n/a (context filter gating fade entries at a moving-average magnet)

complexity.reason: adds an EMA to the trivial touch-requirement primitive

name: ReversalAtDefinedSupportResistanceLevel
quote: Look for reversals at support or resistance areas like the moving average, trend lines, trend channel lines, swing highs and lows (especially the high and low of yesterday), breakout areas, trading range tops and bottoms, and measured move targets.
description: Meta-filter: opening reversal setups cluster where price meets one of several defined support/resistance references (EMA, trend line, trend channel line, swing high/low -- especially yesterday's --, a breakout level, a trading-range boundary, or a measured-move target); a reversal-bar signal there is more credible than one in open space.
pseudocode: abs(close[0] - ema[0]) <= levelTouchTicks*tick || abs(close[0] - priorSessionHigh) <= levelTouchTicks*tick || abs(close[0] - priorSessionLow) <= levelTouchTicks*tick /* additional level terms: trend line, channel line, trading-range boundary, measured-move target -- each defined elsewhere */
book_order_type: n/a (context filter enabling other reversal-entry candidates)

complexity.reason: several of the named levels (trend line, trend channel line, trading-range boundary, measured-move target) need pivot detection and line/measured-move projection; only the EMA and yesterday's-high/low terms are simple

notes: Deliberately composite/high-level: the authoring pass should decompose this into the individual level-touch primitives it lists, most of which belong to other chapters.

name: RoundNumberMagnetOvershootTarget
quote: It will typically go 5 to 10 percent above the magnet before it pulls back, and it usually pulls back below the round number at least once before it decides what it will do next.
description: Round price levels (e.g., 100, 300, or other instrument-scale-appropriate round numbers) act as price magnets: a strong trend approaching one tends to overshoot it by roughly 5-10% before pulling back to retest the round number from above (or below, for a decline toward a round number). Usable as a profit-taking target on approach and as a pullback-entry zone on the retest.
pseudocode: roundLevel = roundToNearest(close[0], roundStep); overshootTarget = roundLevel * (1 + overshootPct); retestZone = roundLevel
book_order_type: n/a (a target/zone concept, not a specific order)

complexity.reason: which round number counts as a meaningful magnet is scale-dependent (a $93 stock vs. a $1.30 currency pair) and is a design decision before this could be coded, not just a computation

notes: Two book examples at very different price scales: FCX at 93 targeting the 100 magnet, and AAPL stalling just below 300; roundStep and overshootPct would need to be chosen per instrument.

name: FibonacciRetracementPullbackEntry
quote: the first pullback in a new trend often retraces about 62 percent of the first leg but not often enough to place a limit order to enter there.
description: Long side: the first pullback of a new bull leg reaches down to a Fibonacci fraction of that leg's range; buy a bounce there.
pseudocode: retracementLevel = legHigh - fibFraction * (legHigh - legLow); low[0] <= retracementLevel && close[0] > retracementLevel
book_order_type: limit order at the retracement level (Brooks explicitly says this is usually unwise)

complexity.reason: needs the leg's high/low from swing-pivot detection

notes: Brooks himself is skeptical: 'most are just approximations and most fail'; kept as a candidate because it is a concrete bar-level test, with confidence marked low to reflect his caveat.

name: TrendBreaksManyResistanceLevels
quote: The trend goes very far and breaks several resistance levels, like the moving average, prior swing highs, and trend lines, and each by many ticks.
description: Price decisively breaks multiple distinct resistance references (moving average, prior swing high, trend line) by more than a minimal margin -- a composite structural sign of a very strong trend.
pseudocode: // combines several sub-detections (EMA break, swing-high break, trend-line break) each by a minimum margin; needs a design decision on how many/which count as 'several'

complexity.reason: combines several hard sub-detections of heterogeneous reference types; needs a design decision on thresholds and counting before it can be coded
